title: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS)
subject: neurology
summary: Rapidly progressive, fairly symmetrical weakness with areflexia: monitor FVC and bulbar function closely (20/30/40 rule), treat patients unable to walk unaided with IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (within 2 weeks) or plasma exchange (within 4 weeks), and watch for dysautonomia.

sections.title: Recognise
items: Progressive, fairly symmetrical weakness of legs and/or arms with reduced or absent reflexes, reaching nadir within 2 to 4 weeks; often after diarrhoea or a respiratory infection in the preceding 6 weeks.
Pain (back, radicular, limb) is common and may precede weakness. Facial and bulbar weakness and autonomic dysfunction are frequent.
Variants: Miller Fisher syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, areflexia; anti-GQ1b in up to 90%), pure motor axonal GBS (AMAN, common in India and Asia), pharyngeal-cervical-brachial weakness.

Red flags for another diagnosis: fever at onset, nadir within 24 hours, marked persistent asymmetry, sensory level, early severe bladder or bowel dysfunction, severe respiratory weakness with little limb weakness, altered consciousness, progression beyond 4 weeks.

Differentials in Indian practice: hypokalaemic paralysis, compressive myelopathy or transverse myelitis, neurotoxic snake bite, organophosphate intermediate syndrome, diphtheritic neuropathy, myasthenia, botulism, porphyria.

sections.title: Investigations
items: Bloods: potassium, sodium, calcium, magnesium, phosphate, CK, glucose, CBC, renal and liver function.

CSF: raised protein with normal cell count supports GBS, but protein is normal in 30 to 50% in the first week. Cells 10 to 50 per microlitre: consider infection (for example HIV); above 50: look for another diagnosis.
Nerve conduction studies support the diagnosis and subtype (AIDP, AMAN, AMSAN) but may be normal early; repeat if needed.
Anti-GQ1b antibodies if Miller Fisher syndrome is suspected. MRI spine if atypical (sensory level, sphincter involvement) to exclude a cord lesion; nerve root enhancement supports GBS.

sections.title: Respiratory and bulbar monitoring
items: Assess the risk of respiratory failure on admission (mEGRIS: rapid progression, bulbar palsy, weak neck flexion and hip flexion) and reassess regularly.
Measure FVC 3 to 6 times a day (4-hourly while declining) plus single breath count; check cough, swallow and neck flexion. SpO2 and blood gases change late.
20/30/40 rule: vital capacity below 20 mL/kg, maximum inspiratory pressure weaker than 30 cmH2O, or maximum expiratory pressure below 40 cmH2O signals high risk of ventilation: move to ICU.
Transfer to ICU for FVC fall of more than 30% in 24 hours, single breath count below 20, bulbar weakness with poor cough, rapid progression, or severe autonomic instability.
Consider elective intubation when FVC is 20 mL/kg or less (almost inevitable at 10 mL/kg), PaCO2 is rising or the airway cannot be protected. Avoid suxamethonium (risk of hyperkalaemia).

sections.title: Immunotherapy
items: Unable to walk 10 m unaided (GBS disability score 3 or more): IVIg 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days (total 2 g/kg) within 2 weeks of onset of weakness; also reasonable at 2 to 4 weeks.
Plasma exchange is equally effective: 4 to 5 exchanges over 1 to 2 weeks, total 12 to 15 L, within 4 weeks of onset. Relative contraindication with severe cardiovascular autonomic instability.
Still walking but deteriorating fast, or with bulbar or respiratory weakness or autonomic dysfunction: treat with IVIg or plasma exchange.
Do not give a second IVIg course for poor prognosis (no benefit, more thromboembolism), do not follow plasma exchange immediately with IVIg, and do not give corticosteroids.

Treatment-related fluctuation (worsening after initial improvement, within 2 months): consider repeating IVIg or plasma exchange. Three or more fluctuations or worsening beyond 8 weeks suggests acute-onset CIDP.
IVIg safety: check renal function and hydrate; watch for thrombosis, aseptic meningitis and haemolysis.
India: cost limits IVIg. Plasma exchange is an alternative; small-volume plasma exchange is used in resource-limited settings but its efficacy is unproven.

sections.title: Dysautonomia and supportive care
items: Continuous ECG with frequent BP and heart rate checks in severe or ventilated patients: dysautonomia causes tachycardia, bradyarrhythmias (including asystole during tracheal suction) and labile BP.
Treat BP surges cautiously with short-acting agents, as hypotension can follow. Symptomatic bradycardia: atropine 1 mg IV (repeat every 3 to 5 minutes, max 3 mg) and consider temporary pacing.
Enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily until walking independently; pressure area care; eye care if facial weakness (corneal ulceration).
Pain: gabapentinoids, tricyclic antidepressants or carbamazepine (weak recommendation, EAN/PNS 2023). Watch for urinary retention, ileus, hyponatraemia and aspiration; early physiotherapy.
About two-thirds of deaths occur during the recovery phase, mainly from cardiovascular and respiratory complications: continue monitoring after ICU discharge.

sections.title: Special groups and prognosis
items: Pregnancy: neither IVIg nor plasma exchange is contraindicated; IVIg is simpler to give.
Miller Fisher syndrome: usually mild, most recover fully within 6 months without treatment; monitor for overlap with GBS or Bickerstaff encephalitis.
About 80% regain independent walking by 6 months; mortality is 3 to 10%. Use mEGOS to estimate the risk of not walking at 4 weeks and 6 months and counsel the family.

sections.title: Pitfalls
items: Relying on SpO2 or blood gases to detect respiratory failure; hypoxia and hypercapnia are late.
Excluding GBS because CSF protein or nerve conduction studies are normal in the first week.
Missing hypokalaemic paralysis, cord compression or neurotoxic envenomation.
Giving corticosteroids or a routine second IVIg course.
Stopping cardiac monitoring once limb weakness plateaus.

drugs.name: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIg)
drugs.dose: 0.4 g/kg IV once daily for 5 days (total 2 g/kg)
drugs.notes: Start within 2 weeks of onset (reasonable up to 4 weeks). Hydrate; check renal function.

drugs.name: Plasma exchange
drugs.dose: 4 to 5 exchanges over 1 to 2 weeks, total 12 to 15 L (about 200 to 250 mL/kg)
drugs.notes: Within 4 weeks of onset. Caution with autonomic instability.

drugs.name: Enoxaparin
drugs.notes: VTE prophylaxis until walking independently; adjust in severe renal impairment.

drugs.name: Gabapentin
drugs.dose: 300 mg orally at night, titrate up to 300 mg three times daily or more (max 3600 mg/day)
drugs.notes: Neuropathic pain. Reduce dose in renal impairment.

drugs.name: Atropine
drugs.dose: 1 mg IV, repeat every 3 to 5 minutes, max 3 mg
drugs.notes: Symptomatic bradycardia from dysautonomia; pacing if refractory.
